"我受到〔敘利亞詩人〕阿多尼斯的詩作《Between Your Eyes and Mine》（1961年）啟發，把關於雙眼沉溺的詩句，轉化為探討飛航旅程中情感與記憶的視覺敘事。動畫裝置作品參照了飛機窗，讓觀眾置身乘客的位置。透過第一身視角，我們穿雲上升，在城市景觀之上飛翔後抵達陌生的地方。對我來說，飛行成為懸置的沉思狀態，提出的問題是：我們正前往何方？外望的眼睛，也向內折返。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我感興趣的，是身體在抵達之前先從高空初遇新地方的經驗。我們對一座城市或一個國家的第一印象，往往來自飛機窗外的景色——從天空遠看。我覺得飛機窗的功能與眼睛非常相似：在出發與抵達、記憶與期待之間流動凝視。我們從高空看見的不只是地景，更是一幅被懸置的情感地圖。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "動畫以無盡循環的跑道作結——飛機持續滑行，既未完全出發，也未真正抵達；旅程在偶然、移動與等待之間迴旋不止。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT：你在電腦上繪畫，以數碼方式製作動畫。可否談談最初是如何接觸這個媒介？數碼繪畫為藝術家帶來哪些挑戰？反過來說，又為你帶來哪些自由？ FYKL：我在大學時期首次接觸數碼動畫，當時專修流動影像。那是2000 年代後期，數碼媒體變得越來越重要。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "數碼動畫的靈活性是其中一項最大的自由，讓我在整個創作過程中更輕易地修改、剪輯與調整；大大減輕了傳統動畫製作所需要的體力負擔。這種流動性對我尤為重要，因為作品往往在製作過程中依循直覺演進。一直以來，我主要從動態與影像，而非慣常敘事處理動畫。對我來說，動畫近乎流動的畫作。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "與此同時，我對類比創作過程的質感與瑕疵，也越來越感興趣。近期作品《我們漂流，直到海洋遺忘我們》（2026年）中，我開始把手繪動畫融入創作過程，其後再與數碼剪輯結合。我所關注的，是類比筆觸如何承載另一種親密、脆弱、實在與臨場的感覺。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我並不把數碼與類比視為彼此對立的方法；我更感興趣的，是兩者之中的空間——數碼工具如何創造流動性與實驗的可能，而手繪元素又如何保留觸碰、回憶與人手姿態的痕跡。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT：最後，在你的動畫作品中，音樂與聲音也在情感基調上扮演著關鍵角色。你如何處理作品中的音樂和聲音層次？ FYKL：在《我們漂流，直到海洋遺忘我們》中，我與 Lucid Express 的 Sky Kung 合作譜寫音樂。我們希望聲音近乎靈性和帶有儀式感，令人聯想到慶典或巡遊的氣氛，例如天后廟舉行儀式或節慶時的情景。旋律大致取材自《花衣魔笛手》的原型，以及構想一則香港異童話的意念。在這種想像敘事中，魔笛手彷彿把所有魚從海中引走，留下一片怪異的情感虛無與寂靜。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "聲音並不直接講述故事，更像一道遊走於作品中的無形暗流，承載著渴望、漂泊、不明與集體移動，開闢出延伸至視覺影像以外的情感空間。"}]
article_text:
Florence Yuk-ki Lee’s practice interrogates the construction of place, memory and identity through animation, installation and drawing. Rooted in the geographical concept of topophilia, her work examines how affective bonds with specific locations are formed and unsettled amid sociopolitical change. Her recent research extends into Hong Kong’s oral traditions and folklore, using tools such as AI to reimagine collective narratives. Across her practice, Lee questions whether a fixed sense of place can be displaced by a more fluid sense of drift, a condition that speaks to broader questions of belonging, migration and cultural continuity.

Caroline Ha Thuc: Your work seems deeply rooted in the concept of topophilia – the love of place – as defined by geographer Yi-Fu Tuan. I’m curious about your first encounter with this idea. What was it about his philosophy that resonated so strongly with you and became a cornerstone of your artistic practice? Florence Yuk-ki Lee: My first encounter with this idea was through an exhibition at the Hong Kong Arts Centre [2018’s Wan Chai Grammatica: Past, Present, Future Tense , which explored Hong Kong’s cultural and artistic identity through the lens of Wan Chai district]. The concept of a sense of place resonated deeply with me and I realised that much of my work and practice had already centred on expressing the emotional connections people form with places – not only my hometown but also places I have encountered briefly or lived in before.

In many of my animations, there are no characters at all. Instead, landscapes, cityscapes and the emotions and stories embedded within a city become the focus of my exploration and expression. Yi-Fu Tuan’s philosophy helped me better articulate this instinctive direction in my practice and inspired me to further develop my work into what I see as an emotional landscape.

CHT: Elephant in Castle (2021), in particular, feels like a direct exploration of the Hong Kong cityscape. A rolling ball keeps moving between solid, imposing urban structures, creating a powerful tension between movement and rigidity. Could you elaborate on that dynamic and what it represents in your personal topography of the city? FYKL: The rolling ball symbolises a sense of uncontrollability – an uncertainty of life. It’s like the capsule balls inside a gachapon machine: you never know what you’re going to get. In the same way, you become like one of those balls yourself, never knowing who will pick you. The ball travels through the cityscape, moving between these rigid urban structures and reflecting a feeling of displacement, chance and instability within the city.

The title was inspired by the London Underground station Elephant & Castle. London was where I completed my bachelor’s degree, and the title came from imagining what it would mean for an elephant to live inside a castle. On the surface, it sounds like something beautiful. But if an elephant were really forced to live inside a castle, would it actually be happy?

For me, that image becomes a metaphor for urban life and systems of aspiration. Spaces that appear grand, secure or desirable can also feel restrictive and unnatural for the individual inside them.

CHT: Your work consistently returns to the imagery of childhood – playgrounds, toys and bubbles. What do these symbols represent for you beyond simple nostalgia? FYKL: These images come from personal memories that carry both tenderness and discomfort at the same time. I’m interested in the emotional complexity of childhood – how certain memories can appear playful or innocent on the surface while also containing feelings of vulnerability, loneliness or confusion underneath.

Playgrounds, toys, bubbles and other childlike symbols become a way for me to approach those emotions indirectly. They function almost like emotional containers, holding traces of an inner world that is difficult to articulate directly.

Over time, my relationship with these memories has also changed. In earlier works, I think I was trying to reconstruct or hold onto fragments of the past. But gradually, the process has become less about revisiting childhood itself and more about understanding how these memories continue to shape my emotional landscape and perception of the present.

CHT: Given the significant changes in Hong Kong over the past few years, your own perception of place must have inevitably shifted. How has this evolution in your personal feelings towards Hong Kong been transcribed into your artistic practice? FYKL: In Elephant in Castle , my focus was more closely tied to my emotional connection with Hong Kong during a period of instability and isolation. The work reflected a personal and sentimental response to the city I grew up in – a feeling of navigating unfamiliar emotional conditions within spaces that were once deeply familiar. The cityscape became both a physical environment and a psychological landscape shaped by tension, uncertainty and displacement.

In my more recent project, Double Blue: An Altered Fairy Tale of Hong Kong (2026), that relationship with place has shifted further into a more fragmented and speculative space. Rather than directly responding to the city itself, I became more interested in ideas of searching – searching for happiness, hope or emotional grounding within states of transition and ambiguity.

The narrative in this newer work is darker, more experimental and intentionally open-ended. It was also my first time exploring the idea of collective animation-making, which allowed the project to move beyond my own personal narrative into something more shared and plural.

I think the shift from my earlier works to the recent projects reflects a movement from documenting emotional attachment and loss toward constructing alternative psychological landscapes – spaces that feel suspended between reality and imagination, familiarity and estrangement.

CHT: Tell us more about your current research into fairy tales: is it true that there are no local tales for children? FYKL: When we look into Hong Kong’s cultural history, we find myths and folklore, not traditional fairy tales. Classic European fairy tales exist in idealised settings to teach morals to children. Hong Kong’s oral traditions evolved differently, rooted in survival, community and nature’s realities.

Even the seoi seung yan [boat dwellers] tell stories grounded not in whimsy but in protection and spiritual survival – deities like Tin Hau or legends of the Lo Ting serve as origin stories, not bedtime lessons.

These tales were for the whole community, to ground identity and reflect on history. But as Hong Kong underwent rapid changes, many oral histories were displaced or lost.

That void fascinates me. It opens a speculative space to ask: how can we use our folklore, landscapes and AI collaboration to invent a new fairy tale for Hong Kong today?

CHT: Could you walk us through your process of working with AI? What drew you to using this technology and what kind of material did it help you unearth? FYKL: AI functioned more as a collaborator and research tool during the scriptwriting process. After gathering material, I worked with writer Jess Lau to further develop the script.

What interested me was AI’s ability to connect different layers of cultural information, local flora and fauna, climate, oral histories, folk tales and Chinese mythology. Based on that research, I asked the AI to generate an original Hong Kong fairy tale, inspired by The Pied Piper of Hamelin but reinterpreted through Hong Kong’s own textures and atmosphere.

For me, the process was less about producing a finished story and more about using AI as a speculative tool, one that could open unexpected narrative possibilities and a relatively objective perspective, not just my own.

CHT: Did you encounter any surprises? FYKL: To be honest, a lot of what the AI generated was generic or boring – so my human collaborator, Jess Lau, did most of the script refinement. But there were a few surreal surprises. For instance, the AI imagined black bats night-touring a cave in Central. That image – wild, nocturnal creatures navigating the heart of ultra-modern Hong Kong – genuinely sparked something for us.

CHT: Why did you choose The Pied Piper of Hamelin ? It’s such a dark story. FYKL: For me, it was pure artistic intuition. The moment I encountered the story in this context, I just knew it was the right fit.

Even though it is a dark tale, its underlying emotional atmosphere felt deeply resonant. The image of a collective population being lured away, leaving behind an unexpected emptiness and silence, perfectly mirrors the subtle, melancholic undercurrents and psychological suspension we wanted to explore. Sometimes, a dark archetype is the most honest way to capture a complex emotional landscape.

CHT: In Chapter 2 of the project, you rewrote multiple local tales together with the audience. How did the outcome differ from your version? FYKL: We opened up a collaborative space where multiple alternative fairy tales can emerge at once. Inspired by Chapter 1, the audience and students stepped in to rewrite the narrative and give the story a new ending through a collective animation-making process.

The key difference is one of perspective. My own version is highly solitary, intuitive and close to my personal visual sensibilities and memories of the city. It is a specific psychological landscape.

The collective versions offer a beautiful unpredictability. By inviting the public to construct new endings, the work fractured into fragments of multiple voices. Where my framing leans heavily into a structured state of emotional suspension and open-ended transition, the collaborative versions brought in immediate, diverse traces of the public’s own everyday hopes and vulnerabilities. The outcome wasn’t a single, rigid text but a shared, fluid ecosystem of images – allowing the project to move beyond my own history and become a living reflection of how we collectively navigate Hong Kong today.

CHT: The tales you’re presenting seem to unfold across two distinct realms: the sea and the sky. Do you have a personal connection to the sea? FYKL: Growing up in Hong Kong, the ocean has always been part of my life. Beyond that, the sea shapes the city’s rhythms – from food and climate to typhoons that suddenly suspend everyday life.

More importantly, the sea became a central element of the project because of the curator, Danson Wong. He comes from a fishing family background, and his family have lived on the sea for generations. He belongs to the last generation of the seoi seung yan before his family eventually relocated onto land. Later, he also moved to Taiwan, which is itself an island.

I think this shared relationship with island geography and the sea created an important emotional foundation for the project. In the work, the sea becomes more than just a physical setting – it also represents movement, transition, memory and a sense of drifting between different states of belonging.

CHT: For the animation installation, you’ve placed the viewer within a space surrounded by buoys and fishing nets. How does the physical installation change or deepen the experience of the animated narrative? FYKL: I wanted the audience to feel physically immersed within the atmosphere of the animation installation, rather than experiencing it as something distant or purely screen-based.

The fishing nets themselves were handmade by Danson Wong’s father. He had not made fishing nets for many years after his family left life at sea. In a way, the nets carry traces of memory, labour and a disappearing relationship with the ocean.

The installation design combines these fishing materials with visual references to playground structures and childhood toys. For example, the bouncing balls trapped within the nets resemble both fishing floats and children’s play objects. I was interested in creating a tension between playfulness and entanglement – something that feels familiar and light on the surface yet also constrained or suspended.

CHT: I have long been intrigued by your series of colourful resin bubbles. They look like preserved specimens, as if a moment of childhood has been trapped inside. Can you talk about the origin of this idea? FYKL: I think that reading is very close to how I feel about the works as well – as if a fragment of childhood has been sealed and suspended in time.

This series developed gradually across several projects. In my first solo exhibition, Broken Heart Pieces Disco Ball (2023) , I began by placing bouncing balls inside illuminated gachapon-like machines. The bouncing balls already carried associations of chance, play and emotional unpredictability, which later became recurring motifs in my practice.

Later, in my second solo exhibition, Let It Sprout Beneath My Skin (2024) at Artside Gallery in Seoul, I started dismantling and reinterpreting the bubble-shaped windows commonly found in playground slides. I became fascinated by these translucent surfaces – they function almost like small portals or viewing devices connected to childhood memory.

CHT: In Where Sight Sinks into Starlit Eyes (2025), the perspective from an aeroplane window makes Hong Kong appear to float, almost unmoored. I felt a similar sensation of drift in your earlier work You built a home in my mind (2023). Is this sense of floating or drifting something you’re intentionally trying to evoke? FYKL: I didn’t intentionally set out to suggest drift or displacement, but I find that interpretation interesting. Looking back, I can see how a sense of floating appears across different works.

Inspired by [Syrian poet] Adonis’s poem Between Your Eyes and Mine (1961), I transformed a line about drowning eyes into a visual narrative on the emotional and mnemonic dimensions of flight. The work is an animated installation modelled after an aeroplane window, [putting viewers in the position of] passengers. Through a first-person view, we ascend through clouds, glide above cityscapes and arrive somewhere unfamiliar. For me, flight becomes a suspended state of contemplation – asking: where are we headed? The eye looking outward also turns inward.

I was interested in the experience of first encountering a place from above, before physically arriving there. Often, our first impression of a city or country happens through the view from an aeroplane window – from the sky, at a distance. For me, the aeroplane window functions almost like an eye: a moving gaze suspended between departure and arrival, memory and anticipation. What we see from above is not just landscape but emotional geography held in suspension.

The animation ends with an endless looping runway – the plane taxiing without fully departing or arriving, a journey that keeps circling between chance, movement and waiting.

CHT: Your animations are created digitally, drawn on a computer. Can you tell me about your entry point into this medium? What are the challenges and, conversely, the freedoms that digital drawing offers you as an artist? FYKL: I first discovered digital animation during college, where the moving image was my area of specialisation. At that time (the late 2000s), digital media was becoming increasingly prominent.

One of the biggest freedoms of digital animation is its flexibility. It allows me to make changes, edits and adjustments much more easily throughout the process, which also reduces the physical workload a lot compared to more traditional animation methods. That fluidity is important for me because my works often evolve intuitively while I’m making them. I’ve always approached animation primarily through movement and imagery rather than through conventional storytelling. For me, animation is almost like a moving painting.

At the same time, I’ve also become increasingly interested in the textures and imperfections of analogue processes. In my recent work Where We Drift Until the Sea Forgets Us (2026), I began exploring hand-drawn animation as part of the process, later combining it with digital editing. I was interested in how analogue marks carry a different sense of intimacy, fragility, materiality and physical presence.

Rather than seeing digital and analogue approaches as opposites, I think I’m interested in the space between them – how digital tools can create fluidity and experimentation, while hand-drawn elements retain traces of touch, memory and human gesture.

CHT: Finally, music and audio play a crucial role in setting the emotional tone of your animations. How do you approach this dimension of your work? FYKL: For Where We Drift Until the Sea Forgets Us , I collaborated with Sky Kung from Lucid Express on the music composition. We wanted the sound to feel almost spiritual and ritualistic – something resembling the atmosphere of a ceremony or procession; for example, Tin Hau temples during ceremonies or festivals. The melody was loosely inspired by the archetype of The Pied Piper of Hamelin and the idea of imagining an altered fairy tale of Hong Kong. In this imagined narrative, the pied piper figure seems to lure or guide all the fish away from the sea, leaving behind a strange emotional emptiness and silence.

Rather than directly narrating the story, the sound functions more like an invisible current moving through the work, carrying feelings of longing, drifting, uncertainty and collective movement. It creates an emotional space that extends beyond the visual imagery itself.

李鈺淇以動畫、裝置與繪畫為創作媒介，探究地方、記憶與身份如何構成。她的作品植根於地理學的「地方感」概念，審視人類在社會政治變遷之中，如何與特定地方建立深厚的情感連繫，以及這些連繫如何被動搖。她近年的研究延伸至香港的口述傳統與民間傳說，並借助人工智能等工具，重新構想集體論述。李氏在創作中質疑，對地方的固有親切感，能否由更流動的漂泊意識所取代，這種狀態亦帶出歸屬感、移居與文化延續等更廣闊的命題。

CHT：你的作品似乎深深植根於地理學家段義孚所界定的「地方感」。你最初如何接觸這一概念？段氏的思想何以能引發共鳴，並逐漸成為你藝術實踐的基石？ FYKL：我最初是在香港藝術中心的展覽中接觸到這個概念〔2018 年的「灣仔文法：過去、現在、未來式」；展覽以灣仔區為切入點，探討香港的文化與藝術身份〕。「地方感」令我產生深刻共鳴，也使我意識到，我的作品與創作實踐，其實有一部分早已圍繞人與地方之間形成的情感連繫——不僅關乎我的家鄉，也包括那些我曾短暫到訪或居住的地方。

我的動畫作品中，不少甚至連人物也欠奉。我所探索和表達的，反而以風景、城市景觀，還有潛藏城市的情感與故事為焦點。段義孚的哲學幫助我在創作中更準確地呈現這種直覺，也啟發我進一步把作品發展成我所理解的情感景觀。

CHT：《城堡裡的大象》（2021年）是很好的例子，就像直接解構香港的城市景觀。滾球不斷穿梭於龐然壓迫的都市建築之間，在流動與凝滯之間形成強烈張力。這種動態有哪些涵義？在你的城市地貌中又象徵什麼？ FYKL：滾球象徵失控感，代表人生中的無常，就如扭蛋一樣，你永遠不知道會扭出甚麼。同樣地，人也彷彿置身機內，不知道會被誰抽中。滾球穿越城市，遊走於僵化的都市建築之間，反映出都巿生活中流離失所、偶然難料、動盪失衡的感覺。

我在倫敦完成學士學位，倫敦有一個名叫「象堡」（Elephant & Castle）的地鐵站，而作品的命題靈感，正正來自我對大象棲身城堡的想像。乍聽之下，圖景似乎相當美好；然而，若大象被迫困居城堡，它會感到真正的快樂嗎？

依我看來，城堡中的大象就是都市生活與抱負機制的隱喻。那些表面上富麗堂皇、守衛森嚴或令人神往的空間，對置身其中的人而言，也可能令人備受束縛、感到渾身不自在。

遊樂場、玩具與泡泡等童年意象一直貫穿你的創作。除了喚起懷舊之情，這些符號還寄託了甚麼？ FYKL：這些意象源於個人記憶，交織著溫柔與不安。我感興趣的，是童年時的複雜情感：某些回憶表面看似充滿玩味或天真，卻每每隱藏著脆弱、孤獨與困惑。

遊樂場、玩具、泡泡，和其他童真的象徵，讓我可以從旁靠近那些情感。這些符號近乎情感的容器，盛載著心內難以直說的痕跡。

久而久之，我與這些記憶的關係亦有所轉變。我在較早期的作品中嘗試重構或挽留往昔碎片。然而漸漸地，創作過程不再只是重訪童年，而是明白童年往事如何塑造情感景觀和感知當下的方式。

CHT：香港近年經歷重大變遷，你對這座城市的感知想必亦隨之轉變。這些個人感受的變化，如何體現於你的藝術實踐之中？ FYKL：在《城堡裡的大象》中，我的焦點較貼近在動盪、孤立時，自身與香港的情感連繫。作品是我對這座土生土長城市有感而發的回應：在曾經無比熟悉的空間，探索陌生的情緒處境。城市地貌一方面是實體環境，另一方面是緊張、不確定和流離失所交織而成的心理景觀。

在我較近期的《雙重藍：香港異童話篇章》（2026年）中，這種地方關係已移向更為破碎與推想的空間。我不再直接回應城市本身，而是探討「尋找」的觀念——在過渡與模糊的狀態中尋找快樂、希望，或情感的依靠。

新作品的論述更幽暗、更具實驗性，並刻意不設既定答案。這亦是我首次探索集體動畫創作，讓作品從個人敘事走向更兼收並蓄的多元形態。

我認為，我的早期作品以記錄情感依附與失落為主，然後逐步改變，近期計劃的方向是建構其他心理景觀，創作懸置於現實與想像、熟悉與疏離之間的空間。

CHT: 請分享你目前對童話故事的研究：香港真的沒有本土的兒童故事嗎？ FYKL：香港的文化史上可以找到神話與民間傳說，卻鮮有傳統童話。歐洲的古典童話透過理想化的背景向兒童說道德、講教訓。香港的口述傳統的演化非常不同，植根在維生、社群與大自然現實的概念。

就連水上人的故事也並沒有建基於奇想，而是關乎庇佑與精神存續：主角包括天后和其他神祇，也有盧亭的傳說，是族群起源的故事，而不是臨睡前說教訓。

這些故事屬於整個社群，既是身份認同的根基，也是歷史的反思。然而，隨著香港經歷急速變遷，許多口述歷史亦已散佚。

我覺得那種空缺很有意思，是新的推想空間，促使我們自問：如今，我們可以如何運用本土民間傳說與地景，配合人工智能，為香港創造嶄新的童話？

CHT：可否詳述你與人工智能協作的過程？這項技術對你有何吸引力？在它的協助下，你發掘了哪些題材？ FYKL：在劇本創作過程中，人工智能所發揮的作用，更近似協作者和研究工具。蒐集素材後，我與編劇劉清華一同開發劇本。

令我感興趣的，是人工智能有能力連結不同文化資訊層次，包括香港原生的動植物、氣候、口述歷史、民間故事和中國神話。我以這些研究為基礎，要求人工智能生成一則原創的香港童話：以《花衣魔笛手》為原型，再以香港的脈絡與氣氛重新詮釋。

對我來說，創作過程的重點不在於製作出完整故事，而是把人工智能視為推想工具，藉此開啟意想不到的敘事可能，並引入相對客觀、不囿於我個人經驗的視角。

CHT：過程中可有遇上甚麼意外或驚喜？ FYKL：坦白說，人工智能生成的內容難免籠統甚至沉悶，因此，劇本的細緻修訂主要由我的人類協作者劉清華完成。不過，當中也有過幾次超乎現實的驚喜。例如，人工智能想像黑蝙蝠在中環的洞穴夜遊。畫面中的夜行野生生物在香港的超現代心臟地帶飛翔，的確為我們觸發了靈感。

CHT：為甚麼選擇《花衣魔笛手》般黑暗的故事？ FYKL：我覺得那純粹出於藝術直覺。我在這種情景下接觸到故事的一刻，便知道它最為契合。

儘管故事有其陰暗一面，內裡的情感氣氛卻令我深感共鳴。一整批人口被誘拐，徒留無法預計的虛無與寂靜，恰好映照我們希望探索的，微妙而憂鬱的暗流，還有心理懸置。有時候，暗黑的原型反而最能如實捕捉複雜的情感景觀。

CHT：到了計劃第二章，你與觀眾共同改寫了多個本地故事。最終成果與你的版本有何不同？ FYKL：我們開闢了新的協作空間，讓多個另類的童話得以同時出現。觀眾與學生在第一章啟發下介入其中，透過集體動畫創作過程將敘事重寫，並為故事帶來全新結局。

主要差異在於視角。我的版本高度孤獨、依循直覺，並緊貼我本身的視覺感性和城市記憶；是一幅特定的心理景觀。

集體創作版本則營造出美麗的不可預測性。透過邀請公眾建構新的結局，作品分解成各式各樣的聲音碎片。我的框架傾向結構化的情感與開放式過渡；協作版本則引入了公眾日常的希望與脆弱，帶來貼身而多樣痕跡。創作成果不再是單一而僵化的文本，而是由影像構成、共有和流動的生態。創作計劃超越了我自己的過去，活生生地呈現人們對現今香港的同感。

CHT：你表達的故事似乎橫跨兩個截然不同的領域：海與天空。你是否對海有特別連繫？ FYKL：我在香港長大，海洋素來都是我生活的一部分。除此之外，海也塑造城市的節奏：從食物與氣候，到驟然令日常生活暫停的颱風。

海之所以成為計劃的核心元素，亦與策展人黃銘樂有著莫大關係。他出身漁民家庭，家族世代以海為居，是一家人最終「上岸」之前最後一代的水上人。其後，他亦移居另一個海島：台灣。

我認為，我們與島嶼與海洋之間的共同關係，為計劃奠定了重要的情感基礎。在作品中，海不只是實體背景，同時代表遷移、過渡、回憶，也是象徵不同歸屬狀態的感覺。

CHT：在動畫裝置中，觀眾置身被浮泡與漁網環繞的空間。這一實體裝置如何改變或加深觀看動畫敘事的體驗？ FYKL：我希望觀眾能感到實實在在地沉浸於動畫裝置的氛圍中，而不是把它看作遙遠、或純粹存在於螢幕上的影像。

漁網由黃銘樂的父親親手編織。自一家告別水上生活後，黃父已多年未有織網。某程度上，漁網承載著記憶與勞動的痕跡，也見證著逐漸消逝的人海關係。

裝置把捕魚物料，與遊樂場結構和童年玩具的視覺語彙融合。例如，困在網中的彈彈球，既像漁網浮子，也像兒童玩物。我希望在玩味與糾纏之間營造張力，造出表面上的熟悉和輕鬆，其實暗喻著受制和懸置。

CHT：一直以來，你那些色彩斑斕的樹脂泡泡都令我深深著迷。它們貌似標本，彷彿將童年的某一刻封存定格。可否談談這個意念的緣起？ FYKL：你的解讀其實非常貼近我對作品的感受——就像把童年片段封存，凝結在時間上的瞬間。

此系列在幾個計劃之後逐步成形。在首個個展「碎心碎片迪斯可球」（2023年）中，我起初把彈彈球放進發光、形似扭蛋機的裝置內。彈彈球本來已令人想到偶然、遊戲和情感的不可預測性，其後亦成為我創作中反覆出現的主題。

其後，在首爾 Artside Gallery 舉行的第二個個展「Let It Sprout Beneath My Skin」（2024年）中，我開始拆解並重新詮釋遊樂場滑梯上常見的泡泡形窗，漸漸被這些半透明表面所吸引——它們儼如微型通道或觀看裝置，連接著童年回憶。

CHT：在《把我的眼睛沉入你的眼睛》（2025年）中，從飛機窗向外望的視角，令香港如同浮起，幾乎失去繫泊。你較早期的作品《心之房》（2023年），也讓我感受到類似的漂泊感。這種浮游或漂泊，是否你刻意喚起的感受？ FYKL：我沒有刻意地從漂泊或流離失所出發，但這是很有趣的詮釋。回望過去，我的確看見某種浮游感在不同作品之間反覆出現。

我受到〔敘利亞詩人〕阿多尼斯的詩作《Between Your Eyes and Mine》（1961年）啟發，把關於雙眼沉溺的詩句，轉化為探討飛航旅程中情感與記憶的視覺敘事。動畫裝置作品參照了飛機窗，讓觀眾置身乘客的位置。透過第一身視角，我們穿雲上升，在城市景觀之上飛翔後抵達陌生的地方。對我來說，飛行成為懸置的沉思狀態，提出的問題是：我們正前往何方？外望的眼睛，也向內折返。

我感興趣的，是身體在抵達之前先從高空初遇新地方的經驗。我們對一座城市或一個國家的第一印象，往往來自飛機窗外的景色——從天空遠看。我覺得飛機窗的功能與眼睛非常相似：在出發與抵達、記憶與期待之間流動凝視。我們從高空看見的不只是地景，更是一幅被懸置的情感地圖。

動畫以無盡循環的跑道作結——飛機持續滑行，既未完全出發，也未真正抵達；旅程在偶然、移動與等待之間迴旋不止。

CHT：你在電腦上繪畫，以數碼方式製作動畫。可否談談最初是如何接觸這個媒介？數碼繪畫為藝術家帶來哪些挑戰？反過來說，又為你帶來哪些自由？ FYKL：我在大學時期首次接觸數碼動畫，當時專修流動影像。那是2000 年代後期，數碼媒體變得越來越重要。

數碼動畫的靈活性是其中一項最大的自由，讓我在整個創作過程中更輕易地修改、剪輯與調整；大大減輕了傳統動畫製作所需要的體力負擔。這種流動性對我尤為重要，因為作品往往在製作過程中依循直覺演進。一直以來，我主要從動態與影像，而非慣常敘事處理動畫。對我來說，動畫近乎流動的畫作。

與此同時，我對類比創作過程的質感與瑕疵，也越來越感興趣。近期作品《我們漂流，直到海洋遺忘我們》（2026年）中，我開始把手繪動畫融入創作過程，其後再與數碼剪輯結合。我所關注的，是類比筆觸如何承載另一種親密、脆弱、實在與臨場的感覺。

我並不把數碼與類比視為彼此對立的方法；我更感興趣的，是兩者之中的空間——數碼工具如何創造流動性與實驗的可能，而手繪元素又如何保留觸碰、回憶與人手姿態的痕跡。

CHT：最後，在你的動畫作品中，音樂與聲音也在情感基調上扮演著關鍵角色。你如何處理作品中的音樂和聲音層次？ FYKL：在《我們漂流，直到海洋遺忘我們》中，我與 Lucid Express 的 Sky Kung 合作譜寫音樂。我們希望聲音近乎靈性和帶有儀式感，令人聯想到慶典或巡遊的氣氛，例如天后廟舉行儀式或節慶時的情景。旋律大致取材自《花衣魔笛手》的原型，以及構想一則香港異童話的意念。在這種想像敘事中，魔笛手彷彿把所有魚從海中引走，留下一片怪異的情感虛無與寂靜。

聲音並不直接講述故事，更像一道遊走於作品中的無形暗流，承載著渴望、漂泊、不明與集體移動，開闢出延伸至視覺影像以外的情感空間。

FYKL:当我们看看香港的文化历史时,我们会发现神话和民俗,而不是传统童话故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "即使是Sei Seung Yan(游艇居民)也讲述了故事,不是基于虚伪,而是基于保护和精神生存 - 像Tin Hau或Lo Ting的传说这样的神像作为起源故事,而不是睡眠时的教训。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "這些故事是為了整個社區,根據身份和反映歷史,但隨著香港經歷了快速的變化,許多口頭故事被移除或失去。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "它打开了一个投机空间来问:我们如何使用我们的民俗,景观和人工智能合作来发明一个新的童话故事香港今天?", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/11.Where-sight-sinks-into-starlit-eyes-02_30_.jpg?resize=694%2C1024&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "在哪里看见闪闪发光的眼睛,由佛罗伦萨·尤克基·李(Florence Yuk-ki Lee)", "credit": "Artomity", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:你能通过你与人工智能合作的过程来跟我们走吗?什么引发了你使用这种技术,以及它帮助你发现什么类型的材料?FYKL:人工智能在脚本编写过程中作为一个合作者和研究工具工作得更多。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我感兴趣的是人工智能能够连接不同层文化信息、当地植物和动物、气候、口头故事、民俗故事和中国神话的能力,基于这项研究,我要求人工智能创造一个原始的香港童话故事,由哈梅林的皮皮灵灵感,但通过香港自己的结构和气氛重新解释。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于我来说,这个过程更少是关于制作一个完成的故事,更多是关于使用人工智能作为一个投机工具,一个可以打开意想不到的叙事可能性和一个相对客观的视野,而不仅仅是我的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:你遇到过什么惊喜吗?FYKL:坦率地说,人工智能所产生的很多都是通用或无聊的,所以我的人类合作伙伴杰斯·劳(Jess Lau)做了大部分编剧的改进,但有几个超现实的惊喜,例如,人工智能想象着黑船在中部的洞穴里夜间行走。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:你為什麼選擇了哈梅林的皮皮?這是一個如此黑暗的故事。FYKL:對我來說,這是純粹的藝術直覺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "雖然這是一個黑暗的故事,但它的底部的情感氣氛感到深深的反射。 一個集體人口的形象被偷走,留在意想不到的空白和沉默背後,完美地鏡頭微妙的,旋律的低潮和我們想探索的心理停滞。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "主条目:在章节 2 关于该项目,您与观众一起重新编写多个地方故事,结果如何与您的版本不同? FYKL:我们打开了一个合作空间,在那里可以同时出现多个替代故事。 1 ,观众和学生采取措施重写讲话,并通过集体动画制作过程给故事一个新的结局。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "关键区别是一个观点,我的自己的版本非常孤独,直观,接近我个人视觉敏感性和城市的记忆,这是一个特定的心理景观。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "集体版本提供了一个美丽的不可预测性. 通过邀请公众构建新的结局,工作分裂成多个声音的碎片. 我的框架沉重地融入一个结构化的情感暂停和开放的过渡状态, 集体版本带来了公众自己的日常希望和脆弱性的即时,多样性的痕迹. 结果不是一个单一的,坚固的文本,但一个共享的,流动的图像生态系统 - 允许项目移动超越我自己的历史。成为我们今天如何集体导航香港的活跃反映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Animation_-A_Stitch_Of_Time-2.jpg?resize=840%2C472&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "由Florence Yuk-ki Lee的《时间的碎片》(A Stitch of Time,Florence Yuk-ki Lee),动画。", "credit": "Artomity", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:你所讲的故事似乎在两个不同的领域:海洋和天空,你与海洋有个人联系吗?FYKL:在香港长大,海洋一直是我的生活的一部分,除此之外,海洋形成了城市的节奏 - 从食物和气候到突然暂停日常生活的风暴。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "更重要的是,海洋成为该项目的中心元素,因为库拉特,Danson Wong. 他来自一个渔业家庭背景,他的家人已经生活在海上几代。 他属于最后一代的Seoi Seung Yan之前他的家人最终搬到土地上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我认为与岛地理和海洋的这种共享关系为该项目创造了一个重要的情感基础,在工作中,海洋变成不仅仅是一个物理环境,它也代表了运动、过渡、记忆和不同属性状态之间的流动感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:对于动画安装,你把观众放在一个由<unk>子和渔网包围的空间里。 如何物理安装改变或深化动画故事的体验? FYKL:我想让观众感到物理沉浸在动画安装的气氛中,而不是体验它作为一个遥远或纯粹基于屏幕的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "渔网本身是由 Danson Wong 的父亲手工制作的,他多年来没有在家人在海上生存后做渔网,在某种程度上,这些网带有记忆、劳动和与海洋的消失关系的痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "安装设计将这些渔材料与游戏场结构和童年玩具的视觉参考相结合。 例如,在网内陷入的泡沫球类似于渔船和儿童玩具物品。 我有兴趣在玩具和包装之间创造紧张 - 感觉熟悉的东西和表面上的光,但也被限制或暂停。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:我很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久很久。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我第一次单独展览中,破碎的心脏碎片迪斯科球(2023) ,我开始把泡球放在照亮的<unk>子类似的机器中,泡球已经携带了运气、玩耍和情感不可预测的联系,后来在我的实践中成为重复的动机。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "后来,在我第二个单人展览中,在首尔的Artside画廊(2024年)的Let It Sprout 皮肤上,我开始拆除和重新解释泡沫形的窗户,通常在游戏场幻灯片中发现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/NZ8_9878.jpg?resize=683%2C1024&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "从我们在哪里流动到海洋忘记我们 弗洛伦斯·尤克基·李(Florence Yuk-ki Lee)", "credit": "Artomity", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT: 在哪里的视线转向星光眼(2025),从飞机窗口的视线使香港看起来浮动,几乎不死。我感觉到类似的振动感觉在你的以前的工作你建造了一个房子在我的脑海(2023)。这是这种感觉的浮动或振动你故意试图提起什么?FYKL:我没有故意提出振动或移动,但我发现这个解释是有趣的。工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由阿多尼斯的《你的眼睛与矿物之间》(1961年)的诗歌灵感,我将一行关于沉没的眼睛转化为关于飞行的情感和神秘尺寸的视觉讲述,这部作品是一部动画的安装,模拟在飞机窗后,将观众置于乘客的位置。观察 - 问:我们向哪里走?外面看的眼睛也转向内面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我感兴趣的是第一次从上面遇到一个地方,在物理到达之前的经历,我们经常第一次对一个城市或国家的印象发生在从飞机窗口 - 从天空,在一个距离的视野中,对我来说,飞机窗口几乎像一个眼睛一样工作:在出发和到达,记忆和预测之间暂停的移动气体。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "动画以无限的旋转路线结束 - 飞机无需完全离开或到达,一场继续在运气、运动和等待之间循环的旅程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:你的动画是数字化创建的,在计算机上绘制的,你能告诉我你进入这个媒体的入口点吗?数字绘画为你作为艺术家提供的挑战和自由是什么?FYKL:我第一次在大学期间发现数字动画,在那里移动图像是我的专业领域。 (the late 2000s) 数字媒体越来越突出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "数字动画的最大自由之一是它的灵活性,它允许我在整个过程中更轻松地进行更改、编辑和调整,这也减少了与更传统的动画方法相比的物理工作负担很多。 这种流动性对我来说很重要,因为我的作品在我制作时经常直观地发展。 我总是通过动画,主要是通过动作和图像而不是通过传统的故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同时,我也越来越感兴趣的结构和不完美的类似过程. 在我最近的作品 Where We Drift 到 海洋忘记我们(2026),我开始探索手动动画作为过程的一部分,后来将其与数字编辑相结合。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而不是看到数字和类似的方法是相反的,我认为我对它们之间的空间感兴趣 - 数字工具如何创造流动性和实验,而手动的元素保持触摸、记忆和人性行为的痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Party_ball-ball3.jpg?resize=840%2C472&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "聚会球 由 Florence Yuk-ki Lee, 从 A Stitch of Time. 礼貌艺术家。", "credit": "Artomity", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT: 最后,音乐和音频在设置动画的情感声音中发挥着关键作用. 如何接近你的作品的这个尺寸? FYKL: 到哪里我们跑到海洋忘记我们,我与音乐组合的Lucid Express的Sky Kung合作。 我们希望声音感觉几乎精神和仪式 - 类似于仪式或处理的气氛; 例如,Tin Hau寺庙在仪式或节日期间。哈梅林的皮皮和想象香港的变化的童话故事的想法在这个想象的故事中,脚皮的形象似乎欺骗或引导所有的鱼远离海洋,留下一个奇怪的情感空虚和沉默。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而不是直接讲述故事,声音更像一个无形的电流在工作中移动,携带渴望、流动、不确定性和集体运动的感觉,它创造了一个超越视觉形象本身的情感空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "李 ⁇ 淇以动画、装置和绘画为创作媒介,探索地方、记忆和身份的组成方式,她的作品根植在地理学的“地方感”概念,审视人类在社会政治变革中,如何与特定地方建立深深的情感联系,以及这些联系如何被动摇。李先生在创作中质疑,对当地的本质友好感是否可以被更流动的流动意识取代,这种状态也带来了属性感、移民和文化延续等更广泛的命令。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:你的作品似乎深深植根在地理学家段義<unk>所定义的“地方感”。你最初如何接触到這個概念?段氏的思想為什麼能引發共鳴,並逐漸成為你藝術實踐的基石? FYKL:我最初在香港藝術中心的展覽中接觸到這個概念(2018年“灣仔文法:過去、現在、未來式”;展覽以灣仔區為切入點,探索香港的文化和藝術身份)。“地方感”让我产生深刻的共鳴,也让我意识到,我的作品和创造实践,事实上,人与地方之间已经形成了一部分情感联系,不仅是关于我的家乡,也包括我曾经短暂访问或居住的地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的动画作品中,许多甚至连人物也欠了,我所探索和表达的,相反,以风景、城市景观、潜藏城市的情感和故事为焦点。段義<unk>的哲学帮助我在创作中更准确地呈现这种直觉,也启发了我一步一步地把作品发展成我所理解的情感景观。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:《城堡里的象》(2021年)是很好的例子,就像直接解散香港的城市景观一样。 摇滚球不停地穿过大压迫的城市建筑之间,在流动和凝固之间形成强烈的压力。 这种动态有什么意义? 在你的城市地形中又象征什么? 摇滚球象征着失控感,代表生活中的异常,就像扭蛋一样,你永远不知道会扭曲什么。同樣,人類也好像把自己放在機內,不知道誰會被拉入。 滑球穿越城市,遊走在堅固的城市建築之間,反映了所有生活中的流亡地點、偶然的困難物質、衝動不平衡的感覺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在伦敦完成学士学位,伦敦有一个地铁站称为“象堡”(象与城堡),而作品的命名灵感,正正来自我对象居身城堡的想象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的观点是城堡里的象是城市生活和欲望制度的隐形;那些表面上的富丽堂皇、守卫森严或神圣的空间,对于那些在城堡里的人来说,也可能是被拘束、感到无身无处。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "遊樂場、玩具和泡泡等童年想象一直穿過你的創作。除了鼓起懷老的情感之外,這些符號還保留了什麼呢?FYKL:這些想象來自個人記憶,交織著温柔與不安。我感興趣的是童年時的複雜情感:某些記憶表面看起來充滿玩味或天真,但每個隱藏脆弱、孤獨和混亂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "遊樂場、玩具、泡泡和其他童真象,讓我從旁邊接近那些情感,這些符號幾乎情感的容器,充滿心內難以直言的跡象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "很久以前,我和这些记忆的关系也发生了变化,在更早的作品中,我试图重构或保存到旧碎片,但是逐渐,创造过程不再只是重新访问童年,而是了解童年过去如何塑造情感景观和感知现在的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:香港近年来经历了重大变化,你对这座城市的感知也必然随之改变。这些个人感受的变化,如何在你的艺术实践中表现出来?FYKL:在《城堡里的象》中,我的焦点更接近在动荡、孤立时、自我与香港的情感联系。城市地形一方面是实体环境,另一方面是由紧张、不确定和流离失所相结合的心理景观。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我最近的《双重蓝:香港異童話篇章》(2026年)中,這種地方關係已經轉向更破碎和推測的空間,我不再直接回應城市本身,而是探索「尋找」的概念 - 在過渡和模糊的狀態中尋找快樂、希望或情感依賴。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "新作品的论文更黑暗、更有实验性,故意没有确定的答案,也是我第一次探索集体动画创作,让作品从个人叙事走向更兼容和积累的多元形式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我认为,我的早期作品以记录情感依赖与失落为主,然后逐渐改变,最近的计划方向是构建其他心理景观,创造现实与想象、熟悉与偏离之间的空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT: 請分享你現在對童話故事的研究:香港真的沒有本土的兒童故事嗎? FYKL:香港的文化史上可以找到神話與民間傳說,但鮮有傳統童話。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "水上人的故事也不是基于想象而建造的,而是关于庇护和精神持久:主角包括天后和其他神,也有卢丁的传说,是族群起源的故事,而不是睡前讲教训。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些故事属于整个社区,既是身份认同的根基,也是历史的反思;然而,随着香港经历了快速变革,许多口头历史也分散了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我觉得那种空缺很有趣,是新的推想空间,促使我们问自己:现在,我们如何运用本土民間傳說與地景,配合人工智能,為香港創造新的童話?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:能否详细描述你与人工智能合作的过程?这项技术对你有什么吸引力?在其协助下,你发明了哪些主题?FYKL:在剧本创作过程中,人工智能所发挥的作用,更接近作家和研究工具。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我感兴趣的是,人工智能有能力连接不同文化信息层,包括香港原产的动植物、气候、口头历史、民间故事和中国神话。我根据这些研究,要求人工智能创造一个原创的香港童话:用《花衣魔笛手》作为原型,再用香港的脉冲和气氛重新解释。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于我来说,创作过程的重点不在于制作完整的故事,而是把人工智能视为猜测工具,从而打开意想不到的叙事可能,并引入相对客观的观点,不符合我个人经历。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:在過程中可以遇到什麼意外或驚喜? FYKL:坦白說,人工智能生成的內容難免籠統甚至沉沉,因此,劇本的細細修訂主要由我人類協作家劉清華完成。 然而,其中也有過幾次超過現實的驚喜。 例如,人工智能想像黑蝙蝠在中環洞穴夜遊。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:為什麼選擇《花衣魔笛手》類似的黑暗故事?FYKL:我覺得那純粹出於藝術直覺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "雖然故事有其黑暗的一面,內心的情感氣氛卻讓我深感共聲:一群人被綁架,留下無法預計的虛妄和沉默,正確地映像我們希望探索,微妙而沮喪的黑暗流,還有心理困擾。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:到計劃第二章,你和觀眾共同改寫了幾個地方故事,最終成果與你的版本有什麼不同?FYKL:我們開啟了新的合作空間,讓多種不同的童話可以同時出現。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的版本非常孤独,依循直觉,并紧密地粘着我自己的视觉感和城市记忆;是一个特定的心理景观。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "集體創作版則創造美麗的不可預測性;通過邀請公眾建造新的結末,作品分成各種各樣的聲音碎片;我的框架傾向結構化情感和開放的過渡;合作版則引入公眾日常的希望和脆弱性,帶來貼身而多樣的痕跡;創作成果不再是單一而堅固的文本,而是由圖像組成、共享和流動的生態。创作计划超越了我自己的过去,活着展示了人们对现在香港的同情心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:你表達的故事似乎穿越兩個完全不同的領域:海與天空。你與海有特別的關係嗎?FYKL:我在香港長大,海洋素來都是我生活的一部分。除此之外,海也塑造城市的節奏:從食物與氣候,到到達,讓日常生活暫停的台風。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "海之為為計劃的核心元素,也與策展人黄銘樂有著巨大的關係,他出生於漁民家庭,家庭世代以海為居,是家庭最終「上岸」之前的最後一代水上人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我认为,我们与岛屿与海洋之间的共同关系,为计划奠定了重要情感基础,在作品中,海洋不仅仅是实体背景,同时代表迁移、过渡、记忆,也是象征着不同属状态的感觉。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:在动画装置中,观众放置在被浮泡和钓鱼网周围的空间中。这种实体装置如何改变或深化观看动画叙事的体验?FYKL:我希望观众能在地上沉浸在动画装置的氛围中感觉到现实,而不是把它看作远远,或纯粹存在于屏幕上的图像。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鱼网由黄銘樂的父親親手編織.自一家告別水上生活後,黄父已經多年沒有織網.在某種程度上,魚網持有記憶和勞動的跡象,也見證逐漸消失的人海關係。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "装置把捕鱼材料,与遊樂場結構和童年玩具的視覺詞彙融合。 例如,困在網中的彈彈球,既像漁網浮子,也像兒童玩具。 我希望在玩味與爭吵之間營造張力,在表面上創造熟悉和輕鬆,事實上暗示受控制和困惑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:从那时起,你那种色彩斑点的树脂泡泡都让我深深迷惑,它们看起来像样本,好像把童年某个时刻封闭定义。能否谈论这个思想的起源?FYKL:你的解读实际上非常接近我对作品的感受――就像把童年的一段封闭,凝固在时间的时刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个系列在几个计划之后逐渐形成,在第一张展览“碎片迪斯可球”(2023年)中,我最初把弹弹放进发光,看起来像扭蛋机的装置内。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随后,在首尔阿尔西德画廊举办的第二次展览“让它在我的皮肤上喷发”(2024年),我开始拆解并重新释放游乐场滑梯上常见的泡泡形窗,逐渐被这些半透明表面吸引 - 它們如微型通道或观察装置,連接童年回忆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:在《把我的眼睛沉入你的眼睛》(2025年),从飞机窗向外观的视角,让香港如同浮动,几乎失去了联系。你更早的作品《心之房》(2023年),也让我感觉到类似的浮动感。回顾过去,我确信看到某种浮动感在不同作品之间重复出现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我被阿多尼斯(叙利亚诗人)的诗作《你的眼睛与我的之间》(1961年)启发,把关于双眼沉没的诗句转化为探索飞航旅程中的情感和记忆的视觉叙事。动画装置作品参见飞机窗,让观众放置乘客的位置。对于我来说,飞行变成了沉重的思维状态,提出的问题是:我们去哪里?外观的眼睛,也向内转。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我感兴趣的是,在抵达前,身体先从高空初遇到了新地方的体验,我们对一个城市或一个国家的第一印象,往往来自飞机窗外的景色――从天空远看。我觉得飞机窗的功能与眼睛非常相似:在出发与抵达、记忆与期望之间流动的观察。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "动画以无尽循环的跑道结合――飞机不断滑动,既没有完全出发,也没有真正到达;旅程在偶然、移动和等待之间旋转不多。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:你在计算机上绘画,以数码方式制作动画。可否谈谈最初是如何接触这个媒体?数码绘画为艺术家带来什么挑战?反过来说,又为你带来什么自由?FYKL:我在大学时期第一次接触数码动画,当时专修流动影像。 2000 年代末,数字媒体变得越来越重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "数字动画的灵活性是其中最大的自由之一,让我在整个创作过程中更容易修改、剪辑和调整;大大减轻了传统动画制作所需的身体负担。这种流动性对我来说特别重要,因为作品在制作过程中往往依循直觉进展。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时,我对创作过程的品质感和缺陷,也越来越感兴趣。在最近的作品《我们流流,直到海洋忘记我们》(2026年),我开始将手绘动画融入创作过程,然后再与数字剪辑联系起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不把数字和类似视为相互对立的方法;我更感兴趣的是两者之间的空间――数字工具如何创造流动性和实验的可能性,而手绘元素如何保持触摸、记忆和人手姿势的痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CHT:最后,在你的动画作品中,音乐与声音也在情感上发挥关键角色。你如何处理作品中的音乐与声音层次?FYKL:在《我们漂流,直到海洋遗忘我们》中,我和卢西德快递的天王合作谱写音乐。旋律大约是从《花衣魔笛手》的原型,以及想想一条香港异童话的想法,在这种想象的叙事中,魔笛手似乎把所有的鱼从海中拉出来,留下了一片奇怪的情感虚无和安静。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "声音不直接讲故事,更像一道遊走在作品中的無形暗流,承载欲望、漂泊、不明與集體移動,開發延伸到視覺影像以外的情感空間。", "translated": true}]
excerpt_original: Florence Yuk-ki Lee’s practice interrogates the construction of place, memory and identity through animation, installation and drawing. Rooted in the geographical concept of topophilia, her work examines how affective bonds with specific locations are formed and unsettled amid…
translated_title_zh: 弗洛伦斯·尤克基·李 李 ⁇ 梅
translated_excerpt_zh: Florence Yuk-ki Lee的实践质疑了现场、记忆和身份的建设,通过动画、安装和绘画,根源于地理概念的托波菲利亚,她的作品探讨了与特定地点的情感联系是如何形成的,并且在地理上不存在。

article_text:
Willem de Kooning gilt als einer der einflussreichsten Künstler des 20. Jahrhunderts – und prägte mit seinem von Alkohol, Exzessen und wilder Schaffenskraft geprägten Künstlerleben den Mythos des ge­quälten Machogenies. Das Rijksmuseum Amsterdam zeigt jetzt die größte europäische Retrospektive des Abstrakten Expressionisten seit vier Jahrzehnten. Muss das sein? Ein "Bro und Contra"

article_text:
Singaporean filmmaker Ang Geck Geck Priscilla’s debut feature “ Ah Girl ” won best film in the Asian Feature Film Competition at the Singapore International Film Festival ’s Silver Screen Awards on Saturday.

The film follows a seven-year-old girl in 1990s Singapore whose parents have separated. Ang workshopped the project at the festival’s Southeast Asian Film Lab back in 2015, and “Ah Girl” went on to take the Youth Jury Award at the International Film Festival Rotterdam. Ang is an alumna of the Busan Asian Film Academy. Her 2012 short “Broken Crayon” won the Singapore Short Film Awards’ best short film prize.

'Dune 3' Popcorn Bucket Has Two Sandworms That 'Make It Easier to Share'

Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat won best director for “No Good Men,” which opened the Berlinale. Set in Kabul just before the Taliban come back to power, the drama follows a camerawoman whose work, family and freedom are suddenly in doubt. Sadat, who has lived in Germany since 2021, made the 2016 Cannes premiere “Wolf and Sheep” and 2019’s “The Orphanage.”

The jury split the best performance prize. Pushpa Thing Lama was honored for “Elephants in the Fog,” about a member of Nepal’s third-gender Kinnar community searching for her missing daughter. Putri Marino shared the award for “Four Seasons in Java,” a magical realist drama about a woman who goes back to her hometown after two decades behind bars.

The Special Jury Prize went to Japanese director Nagahisa Makoto’s “Burn,” his second feature, which premiered at Sundance. Nagahisa won awards at the same festival for his short “And So We Put Goldfish in the Pool” (2017) and his feature “We Are Little Zombies” (2019).

In the Southeast Asian Short Film Competition, Yogyakarta-based artist-filmmaker Arief Budiman’s “Golden Island” was named best Southeast Asian short. The film, which competed at Rotterdam, follows a videographer from Java and another from Papua as they make a film about Papua together. Thai director Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke won best director for “The Bovine Comedy,” a Locarno premiere set in a 2036 where cows have nearly died out. His feature debut “A Useful Ghost” (2025) won the Critics’ Week Grand Prize at Cannes and received a special mention at SGIFF.

German-Indonesian filmmaker Berthold Wahjudi took the shorts Special Jury Prize for “‘Vaterland’ or A Bule Named Yanto,” which premiered in Cannes’ Critics’ Week. Sarah Lingam won best performance for “Flame of the Forest,” about a young nurse who returns home and is blamed for her grandmother’s death. Singaporean experimental animator Exyl’s “Singapore God” was named best Singapore short.

The Audience Choice Award went to Singapore Panorama Programme 2, “Second Life, Second Skin,” a package of five shorts: Shara Tay’s “Kiss Me Climax,” Ash Goh Hua’s “Subterranea,” Syahmi Iman’s “Reanimator,” Leon Cheo’s “Orang Minyak” and Ewan Leong’s “Encik.”

Prizes were also handed out at the SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum, held Oct. 30. “Agape,” from Yamaguchi Shin and Miyahara Takuya, won the SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum Award. The SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum Award (Asian Producers Network) went to Lệ Diễm Hà’s “Dear Son An.” Tong Khoon Mun and Zhou Ke Xin’s “Beg, Borrow, Steal” won the SGIFF Abroad Award supported by Sony, and Sam Chua Weishi and Rein Maychaelson’s “Primal” received the SGIFF Abroad Award.

Earlier in the festival, Indian star Aamir Khan received the SGIFF Screen Icon Award from Peter Chan during an In Conversation With session on Oct. 22. Kore-eda Hirokazu, who released two features this year, “Sheep in the Box” and “Look Back,” was presented with the SGIFF Cinema Honorary Award by Boo Junfeng on Oct. 24.

The ceremony took place at the Singtel Waterfront Theatre on the penultimate day of the 37th SGIFF, which runs through Nov. 1. Launched in 1991, the Silver Screen Awards was the first international film competition to include a dedicated section for Asian cinema.

The full list of winners:

ASIAN FEATURE FILM COMPETITION Best Film: “Ah Girl” – Ang Geck Geck Best Director: Shahrbanoo Sadat – “No Good Men” Best Performance: Pushpa Thing Lama – “Elephants in the Fog”; Putri Marino – “Four Seasons in Java” Special Jury Prize: “Burn” – Nagahisa Makoto

SOUTHEAST ASIAN SHORT FILM COMPETITION Best Southeast Asian Short Film: “Golden Island” – Arief Budiman Best Director: Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke – “The Bovine Comedy” Special Jury Prize: “‘Vaterland’ or A Bule Named Yanto” – Berthold Wahjudi Best Performance: Sarah Lingam – “Flame of the Forest” Best Singapore Short Film: “Singapore God” – Exyl

AUDIENCE CHOICE AWARD Singapore Panorama Program 2: “Second Life, Second Skin” – “Kiss Me Climax” (Shara Tay), “Subterranea” (Ash Goh Hua), “Reanimator” (Syahmi Iman), “Orang Minyak” (Leon Cheo), “Encik” (Ewan Leong)

SGIFF PRO PITCHING FORUM AWARDS SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum Award: “Agape” – Yamaguchi Shin, Miyahara Takuya SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum Award (Asian Producers Network): “Dear Son An” – Lệ Diễm Hà SGIFF Abroad Award supported by Sony: “Beg, Borrow, Steal” – Tong Khoon Mun, Zhou Ke Xin SGIFF Abroad Award: “Primal” – Sam Chua Weishi, Rein Maychaelson

article_text:
東京・白金台の松岡美術館で「粧い眠る 秋と冬の日本画名品選」が2027年2月7日まで開催されています。 同館が所蔵する日本画コレクションの中から、江戸～昭和に描かれた作品を通して、秋冬の季節の移り変わりや自然の美をたっぷりと味わうことができます。

※前期・後期で展示替えあり。前期は12月13日まで、後期は12月15日から2027年2月7日まで。

「これぞ秋！」の作品がズラリ

秋のパートでは、燃えるように鮮やかな紅葉や愛らしい鹿をはじめ、枯れゆく草木やカラスなど、秋らしさが感じられる作品が充実しています。彩り豊かな自然の輝きと冬に向けて深まる哀愁を存分に感じることができます。

前期展示の見どころの一つが、川合玉堂の作品3点です。38歳頃の作品《幽渓深秋》と、66～67歳の円熟期の《空山寒流図》《炭焚く夕山》が並び、画風の違いを見比べられるようになっています。中でも《炭焚く夕山》は、 靄 や炭焼きの煙など、画面の中の空気が混ざり合い、立ち込めてくるようでした。

冬に生きる命の息遣い

冬のパートでは、澄み渡る雪景色はもちろん、自然の中で生きる人々や動物の息遣いを感じる作品が並んでいました。

特に印象的だったのが橋本龍美《雪ん中》（1983年）。新潟県加茂市に生まれた橋本は、祭りや民話に根ざしたふるさとの暮らしを、ときに奇怪に、ときにユーモラスに描きました。

本作では、雪国の日々の営みや手仕事の風景が、妖怪や地蔵、狐、狸などを織り交ぜながら展開されています。寒さの中で身を寄せ合う暮らしの空気、そして、自然への畏敬の念などが一体となり、独特の世界観として構成されています。背景に溶け込んだ雪女（中央右上）など、細部にも見どころが満載です。ぜひ会場でじっくりと見てみてください。

後期展示もお見逃しなく

12月15日から始まる後期にも、見逃せない作品がたくさん。秋のパートでは、華やかな紅葉見物の情景を描いた池田輝方《紅葉狩》 、冬のパートでは橋本雅邦《松竹梅七福神図》など松竹梅の歳寒三友を描いた縁起の良い作品などが登場します。 お正月気分も存分に味わえるでしょう。前期・後期とリピートして、表情豊かな日本の秋冬の情景を堪能してみてください。また同じ会期で「百花精彩 明から清までの中国陶磁」も開催されています。こちらは別途紹介します。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班・美間実沙）

「粧い眠る 秋と冬の日本画名品選」 同時開催 百花精彩 明から清までの中国陶磁 《通年企画》いにしえのエトルリア 小企画展

会場：松岡美術館（東京都港区白金台5-12-6）

会期：2026年10月27日（火）～2027年2月7日（日） 【前期 10/27（火）～12/13（日）、後期 12/15（火）～2027/2/7（日）】 ※前期・後期で絵画作品の一部展示替えがあります。 ※通年企画は2/25（水）～2027/2/7（日）

開館時間：10:00～17:00（入館は16:30まで）

休館日：毎週月曜日（祝日の場合は翌平日）、年末年始（12/28～2027/1/4）

観覧料：一般1,400円／25歳以下700円／高校生以下無料 ※障がい者手帳をお持ちの方と介助者1名まで上記料金の半額

アクセス： 東京メトロ南北線・都営三田線「白金台駅」1番出口より徒歩7分 JR「目黒駅」東口バスターミナル2番のりばより「黒77 千駄ヶ谷駅前行」もしくは「橋86 赤羽橋駅前行・新橋駅前行」のバスに乗車。2つ目の「東大医科研病院西門」にて下車徒歩1分

詳細は、 松岡美術館公式サイト まで。

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good morning!

DNA of thief left on a protective painting cover helped investigators identify a prime suspect in the theft of two Auguste Renoir paintings.

Johnny Depp ‘s London exhibition opens at the Halcyon Gallery, who now also represents him.

Morocco has opened the first publicly funded museum dedicated to over 2,500 years of local Jewish history in the town of Fes.

The Headlines

CRACKED CASE. The DNA of a 29-year-old left on a protective painting cover helped investigators identify a prime suspect in the September 8 theft of two Pierre-Auguste Renoir paintings from the artist’s former home-turned-museum in southern France, reports Le Figaro . That person eventually led investigators to a second suspect and to the admission that the paintings were hidden behind a wall in another accomplice’s home. Three out of four suspects were already known to police for other crimes. The two stolen paintings were recovered in record time, but one, “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano,” was torn and needs restoration, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone told reporters. He estimated both recovered works are worth about $4.7 million. Investigators also discovered that one of the first suspects, age 29, recently visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence with the alleged intention of planning another burglary at the modern and contemporary art institution. The giveaway? As detectives followed his trail, the suspect met with a fourth person known to authorities for art theft and forgery. Police soon swooped in, given the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent,” said Bessone. The two men suspected of nabbing the Renoir paintings have been charged with “theft committed by an organized gang,” but insist they are innocent. The third suspect admitted to receiving and hiding the two Renoirs. REPRESENTING DEPP. Johnny Depp is taking his art career seriously and it seems so is the London-based Halcyon Gallery, who now represent the actor alongside names such as Bob Dylan, Dominic Haris and Ernesto Cánovas, reported Arts & Collection . On Sunday, the gallery teased New Bond Street with a larger-than-life facade featuring Depp’s art, which is on display from today through to November 15. “Johnny Depp is a defining cultural icon with a unique artistic vision. Known for his unparalleled ability to connect with audiences through the authenticity of his characters, an encounter with Depp, the artist, is equally compelling,” said Paul Green, president and founder of Halcyon. “Depp has drawn and painted his whole life and we’re very proud at Halcyon to be hosting his first major exhibition in the UK.”

The Digest

Morocco has opened a publicly funded museum dedicated to over 2,500 years of local Jewish history in the town of Fes, marking the first of its kind in an Arab-Muslim country. [ Le Figaro ]

The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pools are finally being refilled with water, after President Trump ’s rushed renovation left the newly painted pool floor peeling off in large chunks, which the administration continues to allege was caused by vandals. [ The Washington Post ]

The University of Amsterdam ’s museum has returned a third-century BC vase to Sicily, nine years after Italy requested its restitution, and due to its “problematic” provenance. [ The Art Newspaper ]

Influential Berlin art dealer Matthias Arndt has opened an “art salon” in Athens, and says the city reminds him of Berlin in the 1990s for its “spirit of optimism” and creative output. [ Die Welt ]

As his sound installation titled 66 76 26 opens at the Guggenheim Bilbao, Steve McQueen tells reporters, “We live in an era where we talk about AI, we talk about the fear factor—because there is a lot of fear around us right now, with the rise of fascism in the West—and for me, what’s interesting at this moment is the idea of love… it becomes fundamental.” [ El Pais ]

The Kicker

WHERE WERE THE WOMEN? Artist Prune Nourry is bringing back forgotten women sculptors in art history, through her forthcoming show, Visionaries , at the Petit Palais museum in Paris, on view October 20 to January 24, she told the Financial Times . “I was invited to the Petit Palais museum in Paris about two years ago, and walking through its galleries I realized that most of the sculptures represented women—often as muses or models—but only 4 percent of the artworks were created by women,” Nourry said. This led her to research little-known women sculptors from the 19th and early 20th centuries, who worked at a time when French art schools were barred to women. Then, Nourry sculpted their portraits using her free interpretations. In over a year and a half, she made 18 busts of women. This is then put in dialogue with Nourry’s other artworks around the theme of women as mythological beings. The show “is about learning to look in a direction where art history hasn’t looked enough, and also to see through the eyes of those women at that time—to reflect on today, and realize how much we owe them,” she said.

article_text:
The history of disability discourse in the movies is one usually filled with trauma and misrepresentation. Too often, critics explain away the lack of disabled representation on-screen by citing a lack of actors, and when a disabled actor does arrive, they’re a new phenomenon. But disabled actors aren’t new. In fact, they’ve been around since cinema’s foundation, and the proof is in 1926’s “ The Flying Ace ,” which turns 100 this fall.

“I remember [wondering during] my first viewing was how is this dude riding a bike using the crutch as one of the pedals, pushing it up and down?” said Joseph Amodio, who works in writing assistive descriptions for the blind and low-visioned, when first seeing “The Flying Ace.”

“The Flying Ace” seems revolutionary in many ways. Filmed by the little-known (to today’s audiences) Norman Studios in Jacksonville, Florida, the 1926 silent film features an all-Black cast and was produced entirely outside the Hollywood studio system. It’s an aviation mystery that follows Captain Billy Stokes (Laurence Criner) and his assistant, Peg (Steve Reynolds), who is missing a leg. Stokes and Peg must solve the mystery of who stole $25,000 from a railroad payroll.

It’s a silent feature that prioritizes its Black cast, none of whom are in blackface, while giving them romance, adventure, and comedy. Unlike other movies of the period, racial oppression isn’t the sole reason for its existence. In fact, it’s entirely absent from the film. It’s just a movie. Furthermore, it’s less a Hollywood story than an American tale. In a cinematic landscape that so often fails to find the intersection of race and disability, “The Flying Ace” did just that.

Disabled actors have appeared in Old Hollywood features, but most were white. Intersectionality rarely appears in movies of the period (let alone today). And yet while watching “The Flying Ace,” Steve “Peg” Reynolds isn’t just a Black man. Or a disabled man. He’s a disabled Black man. One who gets the opportunity to shine as a funny, intelligent character who just happens to have a disability. Living in a world that wasn’t built with you in mind can make improvisation, adaptation, and invention part of everyday life. The film gives Reynolds room to put that ingenuity to work, treating it as a matter of course. Through one dangerous predicament after another, his stunt work reveals a performer who seems entirely comfortable in his own skin. He has little time for what anyone might think of him. There’s a job to do. And he does it with aplomb. Unfortunately, next to nothing is known about Reynolds’s life today; he died in 1945. Of the six features he worked on during his career, “The Flying Ace” is the only one that’s complete, according to searches of both IMDb and the Library of Congress.

For Lawrence Carter-Long, director of engagement for ReelAbilities International, the chance to give Reynolds a second shot at stardom was intriguing. “I went down the rabbit hole and discovered the Library of Congress restored it, and it’s the only surviving complete film of Steve Reynolds, and I was off to the races,” he said. Reynolds, a Black disabled man with a limb difference, is given a character of substance that isn’t tragic or inspirational. “The thing that really struck me after watching it is that Peg is nobody’s fool,” Carter-Long said.

The recent Annenberg Inclusion study , in its sample of the 100 top-grossing films of 2025, cites that only 6.9 percent of disabled characters onscreen are Black. Yet nearly nothing is known about Reynolds’s life, his other features, or even whether he was married or had children. How did he get into stunt work? How did he become disabled? And what did audiences think of him in 1926? None of this is known. Carter-Long hopes that screening “The Flying Ace” will inspire historians to look into him and answer those questions. “Maybe some folks will come out of the woodwork who can help us find some of those answers.”

“‘The Flying Ace’ is a vital work of Black film history, and its centennial gives us a meaningful opportunity to bring that history back into active public conversation,” said Dr. Novotny Lawrence, director of the Black Film Center & Archive at Indiana University. “By revisiting the film with ReelAbilities, FMDG, and Smithsonian’s Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage, we can explore how disability, music, and contemporary access practices deepen the ways audiences encounter and understand that history.” The IU Foundation’s Black Philanthropy Circle also provided key resources for the project and supported BFCA’s co-sponsorship.

“The Flying Ace” certainly feels like a movie that highlights the best of Hollywood’s history, or at least one that would have existed without racism and ableism stymying everything. “Here we have this film that’s showing how long ago the Black community was actually being represented, and yet I don’t know who knew about it,” said Allyson Johnson, professional voice actor and audio description narrator. “People don’t always realize that there’s already that connectivity happening,” Diane Nutting, Accessibility and Inclusion Consultant working with Smithsonian Folklife, said. “I just think about this film in terms of an all-Black cast, in 1926. All these things that were so groundbreaking at the time.”

“Film history is American history. Black history is American history. Disability history is American history. Music history is American history,” says the ReelAbilities site , and the organization is bringing the film back to movie screens on its centennial in collaboration with the Smithsonian’s Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage as part of the “Culture of, by, and for the People” initiative commemorating the 250th anniversary of the United States.”

The film will run as part of the ReelAbilities Rediscover project that “invites audiences to encounter the film anew, bringing together Black film history, disability culture, archival preservation, live music, accessibility, and public dialogue.”

“The Flying Ace” becomes an opportunity to examine American history through multiple communities and traditions. “As we think about America 250, and we think about celebrating, this just seems like it’s a total fit for what we’re trying to do in telling the story of America through culture and folklore,” said Nutting.

Though the movie was filmed in the 1920s, everyone involved in the project wants to make it accessible from both a contemporary perspective and a disabled one. “For a silent film, music is not the background. It is how the story moves, breathes, and reaches the audience,” according to ReelAbilities. Grammy Award-winning blind musicians Matthew Whitaker and Robert Derke are creating a new, partially improvised live score that responds to the film in real time and is described as a “living interpretation” rather than a fixed soundtrack. This was helped by Filomen M. D’Agostino Greenberg Music School, which “brings live music and the artistry of blind and visually impaired musicians into the center of the audience experience.”

Concurrently, the movie’s audio description was unique because it required descriptions of what’s on-screen, silent dialogue, and the film’s intertitles, the written words put on screen to tell the story.

“It was completely the opposite of a standard audio description writing experience,” said Amodio, who worked alongside Bridge Multimedia. “There was not only no dialogue, but no ambient sound, and that’s what I hadn’t expected. There was no door opening or closing. There was no wind blowing, or crickets outside to indicate you’re outdoors. There was no subway train rushing by to indicate you were on a subway platform. So the watchword of any audio description writer [is] keep it short, [and that] kind of went out the window because the entire sonic landscape that is usually in a film I had to provide in the audio description writing. And Allyson had to provide, in her read, the things that she knows about vocal inflection, and rising and falling, and pacing certain things, saying certain phrases quickly and slowing other things down.”

As Amodio, Johnson, and Carter-Long all assert, they hope those without visual disabilities will check out the audio description on this, as well as movies in general. “I am never going to watch a show without the audio description track again,” Johnson said. “The audio description was so beautiful and lush, and it added so much more to my viewing as a sighted person.”

After premiering the film on October 7 at Indiana University, the team hopes to see this presentation of “The Flying Ace” as a pilot for a much larger project that includes other features starring little-known disabled actors. It’s also an opportunity to ask viewers the question of who gets to be part of film history.” “It’s a collaboration that spotlights so many things that deserve to be in something like the America 250 celebration, but more often than not get left out,” said Carter-Long.

From Black historians to disability scholars, archivists to musicians, film is a global medium through which people learn about the world and each other. Disability, for too long, has been left out of that conversation, let alone the intersectionality that comes from being a person of color with a disability. And the bigger hope is that this screening isn’t a one-off. Carter-Long has several disability-centric movies and stars that people have forgotten; he hopes this series will help viewers “rediscover” them.

ReelAbilities Rediscover brings history, community, culture, and access together to change how audiences encounter a film and recognize whose contributions matter. A century after Steve “Peg” Reynolds took the screen, “The Flying Ace” is finally being given more than a second look. It’s being given a wider frame. And it will hopefully dispel the belief that, then and now, disabled actors don’t exist. They’ve always been here.
excerpt_original: Disabled actors aren’t new. In fact, they’ve been around since cinema's foundation, and the proof is in 1926's "The Flying Ace," which turns 100 this fall.
translated_title_zh: 《飞翔的艾斯》变成100,让一个被遗忘的黑色残疾演员回归焦点
translated_excerpt_zh: 事实上,他们自电影院创立以来一直在周围,证据是在1926年的“The Flying Ace”中,今年秋天达到100。

article_text:
“It’s like a horror film because I don’t know what is behind the door. It’s hard to predict what’s going to happen,” Israeli director Tom Shoval says ahead of Israel ’s knife-edge elections Tuesday.

Like most of the country’s mainly liberal-minded filmmaking community, Shoval is hoping the poll will sweep incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from power for good after 19 intermittent years in the top job across three periods: 1996-1999; 2009-2021, and 2022 until now.

Related Stories

Netanyahu Moves To Get ‘NAZA’ Directors’ Israeli Citizenship Revoked

Hannah Einbinder, Susan Sarandon Among Protesters Detained Outside UN Amid Netanyahu Arrival; Dozens Of Delegates Walk Out During Israeli PM’s Speech

Israel has lived through one of the most torrid periods in its 78-year history during Netanyahu’s third period in office, with the head of the Likud party coming to be viewed as one of the country’s most right-wing and bellicose prime ministers ever.

“It’s very tense because it’s so crucial. I mean, if it’s going to be again the government that is present now, or some form of it, then we’re looking at another four years full of the catastrophes that were that were a part of our life for the last four years, and maybe even worse,” says Shoval.

Watch on Deadline

“It’s in every aspect of life, not just in art or culture. Everything is so fragile. There are so many elections where another party got a lot of mandates, but Likud still came through,” he adds.

Netanyahu’s latest term will forever be associated with the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led terror attacks on Southern Israel, in which 1,200 people died and another 251 were taken hostages.

The government’s reluctance to negotiate to get the hostages back sparked fierce protests at home, as it opted instead for a punitive military campaign in Gaza that has killed at least 85,000 people and razed the Palestinian territory to the ground to wide international condemnation.

The period has also seen Netanyahu and his government attempt to dismantle the judiciary; oversee one of the biggest expansions of the settlement program into the West Bank in decades in a bid to bury a two-state solution for the Palestinians; and go to war with Iran alongside the U.S.

At the same time, Netanyahu has navigated a high-profile corruption case against him and his wife Sara, amid suggestions that he has embraced and even stoked local and regional tensions as a distraction tactic, as explored in Alexis Bloom’s documentary The Bibi Files , a film never shown in Israel.

Against this backdrop, Israel’s film industry has found itself squeezed between censorship at home, as the government veered more and more to the right, and an international boycott as the world reacts to the slaughter of Palestinians in Gaza and unchecked settler attacks in the West Bank.

Culture Minister Miki Zohar has led the charge on the former moving to block funding for films critical of Israel and recently joining Netanyahu in an empty threat to strip directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of their Israeli citizenship for their bombshell documentary NAZA probing military operations in Gaza.

He also moved to defund the national Ophir Film Awards, the Best Film winner of which is automatically Israel’s Oscar submission, after The Sea , about a Palestinian boy living under occupation in the West Bank, won the top prize in 2025.

Shoval’s life in this period has been directly marked by his friend David Cunio being among those kidnapped and taken to Gaza on October 7, which in turn led to him making A Letter to David to raise awareness of his plight and that of the other hostages.

David and his brother were eventually released in October 2025 , more than two years after their kidnapping, with Shoval updating the film to reflect his friend’s return home.

“It was very surprising for me that the film was never seen by officials in Israel, like nobody. At the time when David was still a hostage, even when we tried to set up that sort of screening, the government officials didn’t want to do this, didn’t want to see it. That’s the truth,” says Shoval, who has also spoken out against the killing in Gaza.

“And a lot of times when I showed the film in Israel, Israelis would say to me, ‘Did Netanyahu and his government see this film? Do they understand who is there, who is a hostage?’ And I had to say no… I think a lot of people who will vote against him, will vote against him because of that, the fact that he let the hostages stay that long and didn’t do what he could to have an exchange sooner.”

Bring out the vote

Netanyahu’s biggest rival is former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, who is running under the banner of his fledgeling centrist party Yashar, which translates as “straight”, or “truthful.”

Neither Likud nor Yashar are expected to gain the 61 seats they need to claim a majority in Israel’s 120-seat Knesset parliament, so there are likely to be days if not weeks of political horse trading after the results start trickling in from early Wednesday morning onwards.

“I’m super anxious. Everyone is super anxious,” says a Europe-based cinema professional, who prefers to remain anonymous and is among some 67,000 Israeli citizens to have flown home to cast their vote.

His best-case scenario is that Eisenkot and his Yashar party secure enough votes to build a coalition, and that Yair Golan’s center-left, anti-occupation The Democrats party will be part of the mix.

“In the culture sphere, and the film industry, people are very oriented towards The Democrats,” he says, acknowledging some of its supporters may vote tactically for Eisenkot’s Yashar in the hope of giving him a big enough lead over Netanyahu to ensure he automatically gets the mandate to form a coalition.

Amid the nerves, he is quietly hopeful that the return of liberal-minded expats to vote as well as stronger center-left voter engagement generally will help swing the country away from its current right-wing trajectory.

His sentiments are echoed by industry veteran and former longtime Israel Film Fund head Katriel Schory, who was among 100,000 Israelis joining a demonstration in Tel Aviv over the weekend to protest against Netanyahu.

“We are very tense, of course, but we have generally a good feeling, especially after we saw almost 100,000 people out on the streets of Tel Aviv and more than 65,000 Israelis from all over the world taking the time and money to fly over, just to vote and go back, which is really unbelievable,” he says.

“I hardly know any other nation where such a thing could happen. But anyway, the airport is full of people flying in just for the vote.”

He reveals that aside from voting he and his family will be spending Tuesday working as registered inspectors to ensure that “Netanyahu and his gang will not fool around with the voting.”

A member of The Democrats, he hopes the party will gain around 10 to 12 seats and expects it to be part of a coalition government if Eisenkot comes out on top.

“90% of all the Israeli filmmakers, I guarantee you, vote for this party, including us,” he says.

His other hope is that the Arab parties – representing the 2.1 million Palestinian Israeli citizens who make up 21% of the electorate – will also be invited into a center-left coalition, although Eisenkot has not suggested this is an option as yet.

“Honestly, my biggest satisfaction for the moment is that we see after so many years that all the Israeli Palestinians are coming to vote, and they may end up with 16 members of parliament,” he says, suggesting the move is in reaction to the unchecked anti-Arab rhetoric of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and the realization they need to engage politically to get them out of power.

“I think that eventually Eisenkot will have no choice… he will have to find partners in order to get to 61, and then he may move towards the Arabs and say, ‘Okay I want you in the coalition with me because you are much better than the super ultra-orthodox and you are much better than Ben Gvir and Smotrich,” he continues.

Katriel acknowledges that Eisenkot does not perfectly align with his political beliefs but suggests his straight-talking manner and honesty will be a breath of fresh air after Netanyahu.

“It may signal to the world that there is something new and a different wave in this country,” he says.

Implications for the film industry

It is too early to say what it will mean for Israel’s cinema industry if Netanyahu is toppled in a favor of a center-left coalition.

Eisenkot has pledged to eliminate Hamas from Gaza within 18 months of his election, which signals more pain for the territory’s civilian population, while he is also among politicians condemning the depiction of the Israeli military in NAZA .

His candidate list, however, does feature Eliran Eliyahu, a filmmaker who chairs the Israeli Directors Guild and was one of the few politicians to speak up in support of NAZA directors Abraham and Szor. He has overseen the drafting of the party’s cultural policy plan.

“If the outcome is a democratic liberal government with a culture minister from The Democrats it could have a positive influence on the industry and the boycott, but the process will be very slow. It could take years,” says the Europe-based cinema professional.

He points to the uptick in settler violence in the West Bank, saying the boycott and international sentiment generally is unlikely to soften any time soon unless it is brought under control, alongside improvements for the humanitarian situation in Gaza.

“The West Bank, it’s insane, what’s going on right now. It’s incomprehensible. It’s reached such an extent of violence and terrorism. I call them Jewish terrorists, but they’re basically orchestrated by this government,” he says.

“Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich are really working with them… they took advantage of the war in Gaza in order to escalate violence against Palestinians in the West Bank because the attention was diverted… It’s something Eisenkot has to deal with if he’s elected, but as I said before, I think the situation for the film industry is going to take a long time to improve.”

“I think one of the reasons it will take so long, in my opinion, is that many of the people who boycott, they don’t do it necessarily out of a very deep moral stance, but sometimes more from a very pragmatic approach of not getting involved in this, you know, shit show… they don’t want to be considered as someone who takes a standpoint in one direction or another. So I feel many people just prefer to be away from it.”

Schory is more optimistic on the domestic front suggesting there will be a shift away from nationalist and populist cultural policies, and the resulting self-censorship, but agrees it will take time for Israeli cinema to return to the international stage in the same capacity as before.

“On the Israeli side, maybe we will be a bit less squeezed in terms of budget. Although the budget was never actually cut. What happened was that the emphasis was put on populist films rather than art type films. On the international front, it will take time, ” he says.

Deadline also reached out to producers Yoav Roeh and Aurit Zamir at Gum Films who have been outspoken critics of Netanyahu’s attempt to dismantle the judiciary , while their production Two Kids A Day , exploring the detention of Palestinian children , was one of Zohar’s first targets.

They issued a joint statement in response expressing their despair at the current status quo in Israel, suggesting “it had been taken over by a gang of Jewish messianisms”.

“The current government has set out to destroy its country’s culture, alongside dismantling democracy and the independent judiciary. We have become filmmakers without a country. Not because we emigrated, but because it no longer exists. It destroyed itself in an unfathomable act of suicide,” it read.

“Is there a way back? That is the question we are grappling with ahead of tomorrow’s fateful day. If we do not defeat this autoimmune disease, we will die. Spiritually. But even if we defeat the other side, that is only where the story begins. Our failure as people of culture must become a glaring warning sign. Tomorrow’s results may keep us from going over the cliff, but we will still be walking along its edge.”

These sentiments are echoed by another Israeli professional, also preferring to remain anonymous, but with hope the country can turn a corner.

“These elections will determine Israel’s future and, within our own sphere, the future of the Israeli film community,” they said.

“This community has fought tirelessly to uphold democratic values and to keep open the possibility of meaningful artistic dialogue, both regionally and internationally. We’re keeping our fingers crossed, with fear and trembling, yet still optimistic that we can bring this terrible chapter to a close.”

article_text:
At the heart of the nave, the Main sector welcomes newcomers and galleries that are regulars, notably Bienvenu Steinberg & Co (New York), Lia Rumma (Milan), La Cometa (Bogotá), Proyectos Monclova (Mexico City), Silverlens (Manila) and L’Atelier 21 (Casablanca).

Several galleries specializing in historical photography are spread across the Main sector, including Hans P. Kraus Jr., Bruno Tartarin, Gilles Peyroulet, Lunn, Barnabé Moinard and Serge Plantureux. MEM presents a project devoted to Subjective Photography in Japan. Large Glass brings together in Echoes works by Mario Cresci, John Gossage, Guido Guidi, Mark Ruwedel and Ursula Schulz-Dornburg, placed in relation to historical references in photography.

The 44 solo shows allow works and bodies of work to be explored in depth: historical series such as Dirty Windows by Merry Alpern, presented by Miranda gallery; the photographs made by Stanley Kubrick in the 1950s, presented by Duncan Miller; several emblematic series by Kati Horna from Proyectos Monclova; or La Cometa, which presents a series by Miguel Angel Rojas devoted to clandestine encounters in Bogotá’s movie theaters in the 1970s.

Contemporary work is also on view: Bienvenu Steinberg & Co with Juan Manuel Echavarría and his work on the traces of the armed conflict in Colombia, Elle Pérez, a leading figure in New York contemporary photography, with Public Relations gallery, Nadine Ijewere at Huxley-Parlour and Alejandro Cartagena at Patricia Conde. The eleven duo shows notably pair Ion Grigorescu and B. Wurtz at Gregor Podnar (Berlin), Jo Ann Callis and Tania Franco Klein at ROSEGALLERY (Santa Monica), and Kusukazu Uraguchi and Laure Winants at Écho 119 (Paris).

At the entrance to the fair, five galleries join forces around a presentation of Thomas Ruff. Christophe Gaillard presents an installation by SMITH, while Klemm’s, by exhibiting a project by Viktoria Binschtok, creates a link between the Main sector and the Digital sector.

Key Figures

152 galleries*

31 countries

105 Europe

21 North America

14 Asia / Oceania

8 South America

4 Africa / Middle East

44 solo shows*

11 duo shows*

92 group shows*

* Some projects are presented jointly by several galleries.

Paris Photo Nov. 12–15, 2026 | Grand Palais 1 pm – 8 pm (Sunday 7 pm) Avenue Winston Churchill 75008, Paris, France Booth P01 www.parisphoto.com

title_original: 《告別的年代》：昨夜，我與戲院裡的野鬼一起看戲
title_zh: 《告別的年代》：昨夜，我與戲院裡的野鬼一起看戲
summary_zh: 来源摘录：杜麗安工作的大華戲院，我們也曾在張吉安《五月雪》的死難裡見過，為什麼《告別的年代》拍陳金海的幽魂看戲，或者拍杜麗安與葉氏進戲院看戲，要用那麼廣的鏡頭呢？5 月 13 日之後的戲院，6 月 4 日之後的廣場，鏡頭再怎麼廣也容不下人間的未竟之夢。連續幾晚，戲院打烊後會播起電影，祂們都踩著血的腳印回去了。 這篇文章 《告別的年代》：昨夜，我與戲院裡的野鬼一起看戲 最早出現於 釀電影 。

"paragraph", "text": "在這韶子所寫的《告別的年代》，讀者興許將之視為一部通俗的編年歷史傳記，而黎紫書的《告別的年代》難上許多，它既關於評論，也關於小說，當然也屬於歷史。寫到這裡，我們莫不為小說的恢宏感到昏頭，這可能是多數讀者初讀《告別的年代》（當然是黎紫書版）時有過的錯亂，某程度上也是我對《告別的年代》電影的感受。"}, {"type": "image", "url": article_text:
撰文／黃曦 劇照提供／興揚電影 責任編輯／黃曦 核稿編輯／黃曦

《告別的年代》（The Age of Goodbyes，2026）電影開場，少年在促狹的圖書館廊間，纖手撿起鏽綠色外皮的殘簡。那書擺在恰到好處的電影景框一角，雖在彎下身才能見得的書櫃最底，卻像是洞穴裡的魍魎，祂老早就在那等著我們。

這裡指的「我們」，要回到開場搭配的女人獨白， 「這書沒有扉頁。你有點不相信自己的眼睛，於是翻來覆去地找。可它真的沒有，甚至也沒有版權頁，沒有書名頁；既沒有標明出版者，也找不到作者的姓名。更奇怪的是它的頁碼居然是從 513 開始，似乎這書的第一頁其實是小說的第 513 頁⋯⋯」

這一段敘述，來自黎紫書 2010 年發表的同名小說──書的第一段，揭示那本《告別的年代》的外觀，那謎樣的、從第 513 頁開始的書，是「你」，是「我們」開始讀起的──由韶子寫就，同樣名為《告別的年代》的書中書，開首則寫道： 「一九六九年時，陳金海觀看影片《蕩婦迷春》時心臟病猝發。時大華戲院雖全場爆滿，唯觀眾正專注觀賞影片，無人發現陳氏病發。最終陳氏因搶救不及而當場斃命，此是在埠內街知巷聞，轟動一時。」

在這韶子所寫的《告別的年代》，讀者興許將之視為一部通俗的編年歷史傳記，而黎紫書的《告別的年代》難上許多，它既關於評論，也關於小說，當然也屬於歷史。寫到這裡，我們莫不為小說的恢宏感到昏頭，這可能是多數讀者初讀《告別的年代》（當然是黎紫書版）時有過的錯亂，某程度上也是我對《告別的年代》電影的感受。

《告別的年代》電影劇照／劇照提供：興揚電影

《告別的年代》電影劇照／劇照提供：興揚電影

我們可以想見兩道確鑿的原因，一是電影觀眾若是對小說不甚熟悉，大概早早就被複雜的時間／時空結構給搞糊塗了，二是電影觀眾若是太以電影為本位、戮力刻求當中的符號意義，大概也會被那符號彷彿真只是字面意義給惹毛了。

那麼，對要改編《告別的年代》的電影導演來說，小說的嵌套結構在電影裡就成了戲中戲，然而要對著同一個銀幕分裂出 1990 年與 1969 年的時空，還要能呈現小說裡的一種曖昧、模糊性，僅以「復古」或「懷舊」的美術佈景呈示，絕非鑑古推今的好方法。

要將《告別的年代》改編成一部好的電影，的確是件難事，除論氛圍如何營造、事件如何鋪陳，最為困難的大抵是清晰與模糊之間的分寸，而表演是否能服人也是要事，畢竟也非任誰舉手投足即是一個時代的蘇麗珍。

於我而言，《告別的年代》電影是太過清晰，以致小說本身套中有套、戲中有戲，自體式便重象徵而輕寓言的內裡，在電影裡像是被攤平開來，不僅有紙鎮鋪平，還有熨斗燙過。原先富含紋理的時空結構、文學結構，能讓讀者體察一種超越當前時間的真實，並且在破碎的小說形式裡，反而看見小說家以筆鑿穿的裂縫背後，是寓言作為嵌於象徵內部的真實，而這真實非得要讀者自己提著大紅燈籠尋度不可。

於是，當電影將小說的敘事、結構、符號全攤開來，用一種分析案情的概念，圈套起人物之間的關係、連結，錨定角色的意志、動機，再用便利貼貼上所有符號可能指涉的意義⋯⋯，最後在案情分析板最下列，拉起一道至短三十年、至長則有百年的馬華編年事紀，那小說原本的趣味也就消散了。

電影裡的嵌套僅僅只是人為的運作，過分清楚的指涉也讓電影成為一種和諧，而歷史也就只（能）是屬於死亡，而非信仰死後、甚至是復活的。

《告別的年代》電影劇照／劇照提供：興揚電影

我們的確可以說，《告別的年代》電影以縝密的時間結構鋪排的馬華重要歷史，讓不熟悉馬來西亞歷史的觀眾，可以從魅言般的傳說裡，瞧見馬來西亞華人最早的離散。

比如，電影裡的葉氏家族最早遷徙至馬來西亞時，於林間見到一隻黑影紅眼的食夢貘，祖輩將之殺去，世世代代的男丁便被生不過三十的咒詛纏上。

近年，臺灣觀眾也可自廖克發 《人生海海》（The Waves Will Carry Us，2025） ，見得馬華的百年遷徙史：一顆榴槤砸了下來，青年為拿督公所救，食起榴槤有歸順之意，取名同榴槤之音更為獻祭。

《告別的年代》老年失勢的老大鋼波，其女不也叫作劉蓮嗎？小說裡的鋼波最後是風中殘燭了，電影裡的葉氏祖輩也未被拿督公所救，於是我們可以遙想，食夢貘若是惡獸，祂吞掉的究竟是誰的夢？

小說與電影，都從夢的告別伊始。 為了與亡母和居所告別，少年拾得那本記載秘密的書；少年讀起小說裡的杜麗安，要用一輩子的時間，告別未竟的青春夢；杜麗安再看見葉氏要與他的夢告別，鋼波也要與他的夢告別；就連亡母、旅館店主、瑪納甚至少年的幻影，莫不眾裡尋夢千百度，走到了最後才發現原來自己一直都在告別的路上。

循著小說不斷以「你」起文，愈是讀下去，我們必定會發現一種差異是，黎紫書寫杜麗安的 1969 年時，我們已然進入了故事的時空，愈讀只是愈沉醉； 但在讀起少年的 1990 年代時，我們卻會感到一種斷裂，就像那不是在讀一本書，而是小說家在你耳邊的魅語，誘騙你相信待少年歸來時，你就是少年，我們就是少年。

《告別的年代》電影劇照／劇照提供：興揚電影

我們只能以渺小的方式，看見巨大的時間。而那隻食夢的貘，究竟是惡獸，還是如傳說所聞「若有生靈擋道必為前方不祥」的靈獸，那也是歷史的勝者、時間的勝者才能定義的了。

這本被作者韶子稱之為「大書」的《告別的年代》，僅以被榴槤噎死的女人、取名為劉蓮而半生不幸的女人，將馬華泰半的歷史以幾行字寫就。

同樣地，小說也僅以葉氏在 5 月 13 日後的杳無蹤跡，指向 513 事件與左翼運動的興衰。從第 513 頁開始的《告別的年代》，此前的缺失與其後懸疑的追索，同時可為因暴政而起的空白，也可為一個時代人的遺忘，且記憶本為非線性的斷簡殘篇。

如此留白之間橫生的趣意，我個人認為這是電影未能做到的，而小說還有另一趣味，是通篇還真隻字未提 513 事件，卻提了 1989 年的坦克 。

「那一年事情真多。流年吧，總覺得世道不太好。有一陣每天打開報紙都是中國的新聞，全版白底黑字，畫頁也多，巨幅圖片裡的黑鴉鴉的擠滿學生，後來還出現軍人和坦克，看得人心驚肉跳。」

已經是小說的尾聲，一個理想年代的尾巴，與中國青年的死難相依，是怡保最為風情的大女人杜麗安，即使掌握了半條街上的饕客的胃性、貪客的色心，卻還是在奉請祖先牌位再起爐灶時，困囿於傳統女人的桎梏裡。

我總感覺《告別的年代》全書的文眼，其實是八九後的那句， 「說起來，那是屬於年輕女孩的一年吧。」

《告別的年代》電影劇照／劇照提供：興揚電影

未知明確的時間，我們僅能從八九後發生的一連串事件推敲：大年初一，鋼波的老大哥莊爺死了個兒子；杜麗安把持的平樂居，豬腸粉檔的幫攤女孩挺起了孕肚；與杜麗安自年輕時的故友娟好、決定辭工與女兒跑夜市擺賣女人服飾。這依稀是 1990 年後了，也就是少年所處的時代。

要到小說的後半段，我們才能交雜地在杜麗安講起自己曾送給劉蓮一臺縫紉機，與劉蓮手工製作的那件水藍色旗袍時，憶起 1990 年後的少年，其亡母蘇記有一只藏在床榻下的皮箱。

不過電影的敘述發生的過早且蒼白，比如藉由少年憶起自己的最早記憶、是與陌生女人合影的照片，或者此間未見少年周旋於小說、現實與幻想世界的綺夢，都將小說本身以眾生相見歷史的寓言結構，給真的寫小且寫死了。

而小說透過時間結構與行文上的風格，也塑造出一種懸疑甚至驚異的色彩，比如書中有段關於 5 月 13 日的記述：「陽光在給排列在赤道上的樹木燙頭髮，柏油路上熱氣蒸騰。」

這句話接續在小說中的小說，杜麗安於母親的炒粉檔讀小說的敘述之後；更前面是──我（在書中寫的是「你」）們雖然年輕，卻也明白此前缺失扉頁的「513」頁，這組數字所代表的禁忌之意。

《告別的年代》電影劇照／劇照提供：興揚電影

於是，小說家接著這樣寫道：「一隻昨晚被汽車輪胎輾過的狗，烙餅似的，在路上乾煎自己。」

五月當頭的太陽，金光的柏油路哪能有不歡快之意？但是小說家並不這麼寫，她也不這麼思量，更不允許讀者如此聯想。我們僅能讀到風雨將來的不祥，萬事無波卻暗濤洶湧。

通過小說家的曲折，若真要找到如何讀《告別的年代》的方法，那麼我們當真要成為那一讀書的少年。當書裡出現另一個杜麗安，也同杜麗安見到了另一位葉氏，或者少年再見鏡像中的自己，書裡的少年與被小說家點名的「你」，感覺到這書中書的作者正是杜麗安。

其後的敘述即為閱讀《告別的年代》，或者自個體見歷史、自死亡見復生的方法了： 「那感覺像是沿著迂迴的走廊打開一道一道外觀各異的門，而最終竟通向原處，或至少是一個與『原處』極其相似的地方。」

接在那隻乾煎自己的狗後面，是在最前面提到的，戲院死了個陳金海之後的故事。 傳聞戲院鬧鬼，當時還在戲院當售票員的杜麗安有好長一段日子只能在櫃檯拍烏蠅，而電影敘述的是，有未竟之夢的亡者，會徘徊在死去的地方。

《告別的年代》電影劇照／劇照提供：興揚電影

杜麗安工作的大華戲院，我們也曾在張吉安 《五月雪》（Snow in Midsummer，2023） 的死難裡見過；《告別的年代》只要出現亡者就往義山葬去，我們同樣在《五月雪》裡看見。

為什麼《告別的年代》拍陳金海的幽魂看戲，或者拍杜麗安與葉氏進戲院看戲，都要用那麼廣的鏡頭呢？據小說家黎紫書所言，有時候我們總太過執著於符號了， 5 月 13 日之後的戲院，6 月 4 日之後的廣場，鏡頭再怎麼廣也容不下人間的未竟之夢了。

小說起自在五月花旅館溘然長逝的母親蘇記，卻在屬於過去歷史的六月猩紅裡落成了空字，時間的回返在故事裡卻又是一種層遞，而屬於歷史的足跡呢？

我想，祂是踩著血的腳印回到戲院去了。連續幾晚，戲院打烊後會播起電影，陳金海的幽魂就在那看戲，這是整部電影裡我少數喜歡的一幕。

有一隻野鬼，一直在那裡說起故事。

《釀電影》，「如果月亮背面是汪洋，日光就是生命的海流──金馬 63 專題」主視覺。／圖像提供：釀電影（設計：林雅萱）

月亮是最古早的電視，而電影百年的靈光， 是被迫倒下的巨樹身後，有眾人為祂記憶。

如果月亮背面是汪洋， 日光就是生命的海流。
